edition: Issue 030: one ballot box opens today, one title party waits for Mexico, and one app update politely retires two second-hand Teslas
tagline: Your 3-minute Monday reset: vote, race, and the fine print that travels at full speed. Weekend energy, zero scolding.

stories.headline: Advance voting opens today, and the parties are arguing about whether enrolling is harder than ordering a pizza
stories.summary: Enrolments have closed and advance voting for the 2026 election begins today - with 92.4% enrolled versus 94.7% in 2023, a rule change cutting off late enrolment, and David Seymour calling non-enrolment 'dropkick behaviour'.

body.text: Enrolments closed at midnight and advance voting for the general election begins today, with party leaders among those casting ballots on day one. The Electoral Commission acknowledged the Government's change - preventing enrolment in the two weeks before election day - would affect numbers: as of Friday, 92.4 percent of eligible voters were enrolled, against 94.7 percent at the 2023 election. Labour's Chris Hipkins said the Government would be responsible if that figure is not matched, accusing it of deliberately trying to disenfranchise particularly younger New Zealanders; the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick said the rule disproportionately affects young people, renters, Māori, Pasifika and migrant communities, and called it a structural barrier that didn't have to exist. The Government disagrees: Christopher Luxon pointed to near-doubled Electoral Commission advertising and called enrolling 'pretty simple and easy to do', while ACT's David Seymour said enrolment is a task simpler than ordering a pizza on Uber Eats - and treating the benefits of a free society without doing it is 'dropkick behaviour'. Rollout continues: Labour dismissed National's 100-day plan unveiled on Sunday as a reheat of previous announcements, while both leaders promised bipartisanship after a debate handshake. Election day is 7 November.

David Seymour has finally found the civic-duty bar he'll defend to the death, and it sits somewhere between a cheese pizza and a pepperoni. Ordering a pizza is easy, yes - but nobody closes the pizza window two weeks before dinner. Telling a renter who moves a lot that missing a cut-off is dropkick behaviour, from a government that moved the cut-off, is peak 'rules for thee'. Still, the leaders are so desperate for your vote they've gone from debates to doing bipartisan handshakes - the political equivalent of two exes agreeing to be civil at a wedding so nobody ruins the cake. The good news: voting itself just got simpler than campaigning. That part has remained a two-party mess.

RNZ (Lauren Crimp, 26 Oct 2026): enrolments closed and advance voting began Monday 26 October; 92.4% of eligible voters enrolled as of Friday 23 October, versus 94.7% at the 2023 election; the Electoral Commission acknowledged the Government's change preventing enrolment in the two weeks leading up to election day would impact numbers; Hipkins said failing to reach the 2023 enrolment figure would be 'an indictment on this Government, who have deliberately tried to disenfranchise people, particularly younger New Zealanders'; Swarbrick called the rule a structural barrier disproportionately affecting young people, renters, Māori, Pasifika and migrant communities; Luxon cited 'almost a doubling' of Electoral Commission advertising around turnout and enrolment and called enrolment 'pretty simple and easy to do'; Seymour called enrolment 'a task simpler than ordering a pizza on Uber Eats' and failure to enrol 'dropkick behaviour'. RNZ also reported (25-26 Oct 2026) National's re-election 100-day plan released Sunday, Seymour refusing to pre-negotiate, and the leaders' debate ending in a Hipkins-Luxon handshake with agreement to sit down within the first 100 days of the next term. Election day: 7 November.

stories.headline: The kid wins again: Antonelli dominates the US Grand Prix - and his title party has to wait a week
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli won the United States Grand Prix from pole on a flawless one-stop, taking his ninth win of 2026 and stretching his lead to 123 points - but Russell's eighth place means the title call waits for Mexico; Liam Lawson banked ninth with a quiet one-stopper.

body.text: Kimi Antonelli won the United States Grand Prix from pole, controlling the race on a one-stop strategy and finishing 13 seconds clear of Charles Leclerc, with Max Verstappen third and Lewis Hamilton fourth. The win was his ninth of the season and put another 25 points on the board - but the coronation has to wait: George Russell finished eighth in the second Mercedes, and Antonelli needed him ninth or lower (and Hamilton fifth or lower) to mathematically seal the title in Austin. Ninth place at next Sunday's Mexican Grand Prix will now be enough. Liam Lawson capped a clean weekend with ninth for Racing Bulls in a largely uneventful one-stopper, banking more points on a weekend when his team's aerodynamic upgrades looked strong. Russell served a five-second penalty for gaining an advantage outside track limits, and a virtual safety car followed Valtteri Bottas's stranded Cadillac.

Kimi Antonelli has now won nine races and still cannot get his own victory party scheduled, because the maths keeps whispering 'the best man is only eighth'. He is so on top of things that Mercedes could probably clinch the constructors' title by faxing in a result slip. Meanwhile Liam Lawson keeps doing the actual job - tyres on the paint, points on the board, no drama - while the paddock keeps talking about his future with the intensity of flatmates re-organising the fridge at midnight. One more week, Kimi: ninth place in Mexico and you can hang up the sombrero. Pack it early.

Speedcafe (26 Oct 2026) race report: Antonelli won the US GP from pole, leading from the start, surrendering the lead during the pit-stop cycle and reclaiming it with 24 laps remaining, for his ninth win of 2026 and a 123-point championship lead with five rounds remaining; final classification: Antonelli (1 stop), Leclerc +13.078s (2 stops), Verstappen +17.485s (2 stops), Hamilton, Norris, Hadjar, Piastri, Russell (8th), Lawson (9th, +1:19.183, 1 stop), Gasly (10th). RacingNews365 (26 Oct 2026): the title was not clinched because Russell finished 8th (needed 9th or lower) and Hamilton 4th (needed 5th or lower); a 9th-place finish at the Mexican GP (1 Nov) will seal the title; a virtual safety car followed Bottas stopping; per AutoHebdo (26 Oct 2026), Russell received a five-second penalty for gaining an advantage outside track limits. Stuff (26 Oct 2026) led its sport coverage with 'Antonelli wins again as Lawson executes one stop strategy for more points', confirming Lawson started P9 and finished P9 with a one-stop run.

stories.headline: Tesla flips an app switch, kills fast charging on two second-hand cars, and the court says that's fine
stories.summary: Peter Goodricke bought two written-off Teslas at a Turners auction; when he synced the app, Tesla remotely disabled their fast-charging over fire-safety concerns - and his legal challenges have now all been dismissed.

body.text: Peter Goodricke bought two damaged, second-hand Teslas at a Turners auction - and when he switched on the app and software updates downloaded, Tesla remotely disabled the fast-charging function on both cars, including access to its Supercharger network, because it considered the written-off vehicles unsafe to charge in case the batteries caught fire. The move follows Tesla's 'unsupported vehicle policy' for written-off cars, fine print that is apparently easy to miss in an auction yard. Goodricke challenged the decision in the Disputes Tribunal, which dismissed his claim over alleged breaches of consumer and fair trading law; a request for a rehearing failed, and now the High Court has dismissed his application for judicial review. Tesla's lawyer acknowledged the company had no unilateral right to alter the functionality of a Tesla once it belonged to someone else and that it must be able to point to a lawful entitlement to do so - but the judge found Goodricke's claim that Tesla publicly maintained its cars would keep fast-charging access throughout their working lives was incorrect.

Welcome to 2026, where even the car you own outright can be quietly edited by its manufacturer, like Wikipedia for motorists. New phrase to file away: 'unsupported vehicle policy' - the automotive equivalent of 'we reserve the right to change the terms while you sleep'. Everything is a service now, including the physical thing you paid for with actual dollars. Legally the judge's reading is neat: if the papers didn't promise forever, the kill switch stands. But we suspect 'your new car may be remotely retired' isn't the line buyers imagine when they read the warranty - mainly because nobody reads the warranty, especially the one stapled to a Turners auction yard. To be fair to Tesla: a damaged battery that might catch fire is a genuine safety call. All we ask is it go on the auction sticker, right under the odometer reading, in the same font they use for 'no returns'.

NZ Herald, Open Justice (Tracy Neal, 25 Oct 2026, 9pm): Peter Goodricke bought two written-off Teslas second-hand at a Turners auction; fast charging on both vehicles, including Supercharger access, was remotely disabled once he used the Tesla app and software updates downloaded, under the manufacturer's unsupported vehicle policy for written-off cars pending assessment of fire or other damage risk; the Disputes Tribunal dismissed his claim over alleged breaches of consumer and fair trading law and a subsequent rehearing was also dismissed; the High Court dismissed his application for judicial review; Tesla's lawyer acknowledged the company had no unilateral right to alter the functionality of a Tesla vehicle once it belonged to someone else and must be able to point to a lawful entitlement to do so; the judge said Goodricke's case rested on the proposition that Tesla publicly maintained vehicles would have access to fast-charging networks throughout their working lives, and that proposition was incorrect.

affiliate_cta.headline: Voting today, racing next weekend, two Teslas charging politely - a calm pause before you decide.
affiliate_cta.body: Election day is coming, Mexico City is next Sunday, and the fine print is full of surprises. No pitch, just a calm nudge to sort the small practical stuff - check the enrolment link, set an alarm for the race, maybe glance at a warranty - so the week starts soft and nothing sneaks up on you.
